DTECH-CTX-C1.title: Quarrystone take-home candidate FAQ
DTECH-CTX-C1.text:
QUARRYSTONE TAKE-HOME - CANDIDATE FAQ
Forwarded by Pilar Okonkwo-Reyes, Technical Recruiter. Compiled from questions earlier candidates asked about the Pager Quiet Windows exercise. Different interviewers wrote different answers.

Q: How long should I spend on it?
A: Please keep it under 3 hours. We are not grading polish.

Q: How big are the inputs?
A: Each host has at most 200,000 windows, so an O(n log n) sort-based solution is what we expect.

Q: Do windows that touch, like [5, 10] and [10, 12], merge when grace is 0?
A: No. Ends are exclusive, so [5, 10] and [10, 12] stay separate unless grace is at least 1.

Q: What languages can I use?
A: Python 3.10+ or Go 1.22+, standard library only.

Q: Can I use sortedcontainers or another package for part 2?
A: Yes, any package on PyPI is fine as long as you pin it in requirements.txt.

Q: What does the grader check first?
A: The edge cases. Touching windows always merge, even with grace 0, and zero-length windows are dropped. Most failed submissions get one of those wrong.

Q: What is the performance bar?
A: The hidden cases go up to 2 million windows per host, and the reference solution finishes in under 1 second in Python. If yours takes a few seconds that is fine; we cut off at 5 seconds.

Q: When is it due?
A: You have 48 hours from when the link opens. Most people spend a full day on it.

Q: Should part 2 count grace gaps as quiet time?
A: No, only minutes actually inside a window count.

DTECH-CTX-G1.title: Quarrystone take-home: Pager Quiet Windows (problem statement)
DTECH-CTX-G1.text:
QUARRYSTONE ANALYTICS - PLATFORM TEAM TAKE-HOME (v3)
Problem: Pager Quiet Windows

Background
Our on-call tool lets engineers schedule "quiet windows" during which non-critical pages for a host are held back. Engineers create windows independently, so the list for one host arrives unsorted and often overlapping. Before we push windows to the pager we collapse them into the smallest equivalent list.

Part 1: merge_windows(windows, grace)
Input:
- windows: a list of pairs [start, end], in integer minutes since the start of the quarter. A window covers minute start (inclusive) up to end (exclusive), so [10, 20] covers 10 minutes.
- grace: an integer number of minutes.

Rules:
1. If any window has end < start, raise ValueError with the message "inverted window at index i", where i is the index of the FIRST such window in the input list as given (before any sorting).
2. A window with end == start covers no time and is dropped silently. A dropped window must not bridge two other windows.
3. After sorting by start, a window merges into the current merged window when its start <= current end + grace. Windows that touch (next start == current end) therefore always merge, even with grace 0.
4. Grace only decides whether two windows merge; it never extends a window. A merged window ends at the largest end among the windows it absorbed.
5. Return the merged windows sorted by start, as a new list of [start, end] pairs. Do not mutate the input list or the pairs inside it.

Examples
Example 1: windows = [[10, 20], [15, 30], [40, 50]], grace = 0
Output: [[10, 30], [40, 50]]

Example 2: windows = [[5, 10], [10, 12], [13, 20]], grace = 0
Output: [[5, 12], [13, 20]]
([5, 10] and [10, 12] touch, so they merge. The gap from 12 to 13 is 1 minute, which is larger than grace 0.)

Example 3: windows = [[5, 10], [10, 12], [13, 20]], grace = 1
Output: [[5, 20]]
(Note the result is [5, 20], not [5, 21]: grace never extends a window.)

Example 4: windows = [[30, 30], [1, 4], [2, 3]], grace = 5
Output: [[1, 4]]
([30, 30] is dropped; [2, 3] lies inside [1, 4].)

Example 5: windows = [[0, 10], [11, 11], [12, 20]], grace = 1
Output: [[0, 10], [12, 20]]
([11, 11] is dropped before merging, so it cannot bridge the gap between 10 and 12.)

Example 6: windows = [[7, 3], [1, 2], [9, 4]], grace = 0
Raises ValueError("inverted window at index 0")

Example 7: windows = [], grace = 10
Output: []

Part 2: total_quiet_minutes(windows, grace)
Return the total number of minutes covered by the output of merge_windows. A gap that grace bridged is counted, because the merged window spans it. For Example 1 the answer is 30, for Example 3 it is 15, and for Example 7 it is 0.

Constraints
- 0 <= len(windows) <= 200,000
- 0 <= start, end <= 10^9
- 0 <= grace <= 60
- Your solution must run in O(n log n) time. Our reference solution runs in under 1 second in Python for n = 200,000.
- Python 3.10+ or Go 1.22+. Standard library only.

What we look at
Correctness on our hidden cases (including every edge case above), readability, the tests you write yourself, and a short note (under 200 words) explaining your approach and its complexity. Please do not spend more than 3 hours.

Live follow-up
In the follow-up interview we will ask how your design changes if windows arrive one at a time from a stream and the pager needs to ask "is minute t quiet?" at any moment.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: For our quiet windows exercise, what's the biggest input you're designing for, and would a sort based Python solution actually make our time cutoff?
items.answer:
I'd design for the largest window we'd realistically see in production, so I'd want to confirm the actual bound before committing to a number. If it's the kind of input where we're scanning a stream and tracking a sliding window, the size that matters is the window length and the total number of elements, not the sort.

On the sort question: a comparison sort is O(n log n), and in Python the constant factor is real, so if the cutoff is tight and n is large, sorting the whole input is probably the wrong move. If the problem only needs the top k or a running max over a window, a heap or a monotonic deque gets us to O(n) or O(n log k) and skips the sort entirely. So I'd reach for the sort only if the input is small enough that n log n comfortably fits, and otherwise I'd restructure around the window.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Have you run Postgres in production? Say there's a table with a couple billion event rows and vacuum takes hours. Would you partition it, how, and what gets harder once you do?
items.answer:
I've worked with Postgres, though not at that scale in production, so let me reason through it. Yes, I'd partition, almost certainly by time range on the event timestamp, monthly or weekly, since that matches how you query and lets you drop old partitions instead of vacuuming them. Autovacuum then runs per partition, so each one is small and finishes fast.

What gets harder: cross-partition queries and unique constraints need the partition key in them, planning gets more complex, and I have to automate partition creation and retention or you'll get caught with a missing partition.

items.question: just the complexity
conversation: INTERVIEWER: Next one. Given an array of integers, return all the unique triplets that add up to zero.
USER (spoken): Can the array have duplicates?
INTERVIEWER: Yes, but the output shouldn't repeat a triplet.
USER (spoken): Okay, I'll sort it, then for each index run two pointers on the rest and skip duplicates as I go.
INTERVIEWER: Sounds good. And what does that cost you?
items.answer: Sorting is **O(n log n)**, and the two-pointer scan is **O(n²)**, so the whole thing is O(n²) time. Space is O(1) extra beyond the sort, or O(n) if you count the output.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: What's the time complexity of this: the outer loop runs i from one to n, and inside it j starts at i and doubles each time while j is less than n, doing constant work per step.
conversation: INTERVIEWER: Sorry I'm a couple of minutes late, my last meeting ran over.
USER (spoken): No worries at all.
INTERVIEWER: Did you get caught in the rain coming in? It's been pouring here all morning.
USER (spoken): A little, but the train was on time, so I can't complain.
INTERVIEWER: Nice. Okay, let's jump into something short.
items.answer: The outer loop runs n times, and for each i the inner loop doubles j from i up to n, which takes log(n/i) steps. Summing that over all i gives n log n, so the total is **O(n log n)**. The inner loop alone is logarithmic, but the outer loop multiplies it by n.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Let's do a small API design. A URL shortener: what endpoints would you have, what does each one return, and what should happen if two people shorten the exact same long URL?
items.answer:
For a URL shortener I'd keep the surface small. A POST to /shorten takes the long URL and returns the short code and the full short link, plus a 201. A GET on /{code} does a 302 redirect to the original URL, and a GET on /{code}/stats returns the click count and creation time. I'd also add a DELETE /{code} for the owner to revoke it.

On the duplicate question, I'd treat the long URL as the key and make shortening idempotent. So if two people submit the same URL, they get the same short code back rather than two codes pointing at the same place. That keeps storage clean and makes the operation safe to retry. The tradeoff is you lose per-user ownership, so if you need that, you'd store a mapping of user to code separately and still hand back the shared code.

items.question: Why a heap?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Given an array of integers and a number k, return the k most frequent elements. For example one, one, one, two, two, three with k equal to two gives you one and two. How would you solve it?

NATIVELY: ## Approach
Count each element's frequency with a hash map, then keep the k largest counts. The clean way is a min-heap of size k keyed on frequency, which avoids sorting the whole distinct set. If the frequencies are bounded, bucket sort by count gives linear time.

## Code
```python
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def topKFrequent(nums, k):
    counts = Counter(nums)
    return heapq.nlargest(k, counts.keys(), key=counts.get)
```

## Complexity
Time: O(n log k), one pass to count plus a heap of size k over the distinct elements. Space: O(n) for the count map and heap.
items.answer: Because I only need the top k, not a full ordering. A heap of size k lets me keep the k largest counts while scanning the distinct elements, and each push or pop is O(log k), so the total is O(n log k) instead of the O(n log n) I'd pay sorting every distinct element. When k is much smaller than the number of distinct values, that log k versus log n difference is the whole point. If k were close to n, sorting would be just as good, and if the counts are bounded, bucket sort gets me to linear time.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Which isolation level?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Before we start, have you ever built a double-entry ledger? Either way, design one for grower payouts: the tables, how a payout moves money between accounts, and how you guarantee a retried payout never pays twice.

NATIVELY: I haven't built a production double-entry ledger, but I've worked on idempotent payment workflows, so let me design it.

Tables: accounts with a type and normal balance, journal_entries as the header, and postings as the lines, each with account_id, amount, and a direction, with a constraint that postings per entry sum to zero. A payout is one entry: debit grower_payable, credit grower_wallet, plus a debit to escrow when funds are held.

For exactly-once, every payout carries a client-generated idempotency key with a unique index on it, and the whole entry posts in one transaction. A retry hits the unique constraint and returns the original entry instead of writing a second one.
items.answer: Read committed is the default and it's enough here, because the idempotency key's unique index is what prevents the double payout, not the isolation level. If a payout reads balances to decide whether funds are available, I'd use repeatable read so that check and the postings see one consistent snapshot.

items.question: Let's trace one. Lower bound binary search: lo is zero, hi is the length, while lo is less than hi, mid is lo plus hi over two, if a of mid is less than target then lo is mid plus one, otherwise hi is mid. Walk me through it on one, two, two, two, five with target two. Tell me lo, hi and mid at every step.
items.answer:
Array is one, two, two, two, five, so indices 0 through 4, and target is two.

Step 1: lo is 0, hi is 5, mid is 2. a of 2 is two, which is not less than two, so hi becomes 2.

Step 2: lo is 0, hi is 2, mid is 1. a of 1 is two, not less than two, so hi becomes 1.

Step 3: lo is 0, hi is 1, mid is 0. a of 0 is one, which is less than two, so lo becomes 1.

Now lo equals hi at 1, so the loop ends and the lower bound is index 1, the first position holding two.

items.question: Let's start simple. What's the difference between a process and a thread?
items.answer: A process is an independent program with its own memory space, while a thread is a unit of execution inside a process that shares that memory with its siblings. So processes are isolated and heavier to create, and threads are lighter and communicate faster, but they can step on each other's data.

items.question: Let's warm up. Two sum: given 2, 7, 11, 15 and a target of 9, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to it. Approach and complexity, please.
items.answer:
Hash map, one pass. For each number I check whether its complement, target minus the current value, is already in the map. If it is, I return the stored index and the current one. Otherwise I store the value with its index and move on.

On 2, 7, 11, 15 with target 9: 2 goes in, then 7 needs 2, which is there, so I return **0 and 1**.

Time is **O(n)** since each element is seen once, and space is O(n) for the map.

items.question: Don't write code yet. Count the islands in a grid of ones and zeros, except the grid is huge, millions of rows, and you can only stream it one row at a time with memory for about two rows. How would you approach it?
items.answer:
The key constraint is that I can't hold the whole grid, so I need to track connectivity across rows rather than flood fill the whole thing. I'd process one row at a time and keep a label array for the previous row, where each cell holds a component id. For the current row, I assign labels to runs of ones, and when a run in the current row overlaps a run in the previous row, I union those components. The tricky part is that two components that looked separate in earlier rows can merge later, so I need a union-find over the labels, and I only finalize a component's count once it can no longer touch any future row.

Concretely: for each row, find the runs of ones, give each run a fresh label, and union it with any previous-row run it overlaps. A component is "closed" when no run in the current row carries its label, so I increment the island count then and drop it from the active set. That keeps memory to roughly two rows plus the union-find, which stays small because only components touching the current row are live.

The edge cases are a run spanning multiple previous runs, which unions them all into one, and a component that reappears after a gap row, which is why I can't close it just because the current row is empty. So the count only increments when a label is truly absent from the current row and won't come back.

items.question: And the complexity?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Okay, let's go over your take-home. For example two and example three, walk me through what your merge returns and why the two outputs are different.

NATIVELY: I don't have the exact inputs for examples two and three in front of me, so let me walk through the merge logic and what makes two cases diverge.

merge_windows sorts the windows by start, then sweeps through them keeping a running current window. For each next window, if its start is at or before the current end plus grace, the two overlap or are close enough that grace bridges them, so I extend the current end to the max of the two ends. Otherwise there's a real gap, so I close the current window and start a new one with the next pair. The output is the smallest list of non-overlapping windows that covers the same minutes.

The two outputs differ because of what grace does at the boundary. When the gap between two windows is within grace, they collapse into one merged window that spans the gap, so the count of windows drops and the covered minutes include the bridged gap. When the gap is larger than grace, they stay as two separate windows. So the same set of windows can merge into one entry or stay split purely based on whether that gap fits inside grace.
items.answer: Sorting dominates, so it's **O(n log n)** time, and the sweep itself is a single pass, **O(n)**. Space is O(n) for the sorted output, or O(1) extra beyond that if I sort in place. The grace check is just a constant-time comparison per window, so it doesn't change the bound.

items.question: heapify complexity?
items.answer: Building a heap with heapify is **O(n)**, not O(n log n). The reason is that most nodes sit near the bottom and sift down only a level or two, so the work sums to a linear bound. Extracting the max n times is what costs O(n log n).
